title: What makes demand elastic or inelastic

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify the determinants of PED - substitutes, the share of income the purchase takes, necessity against luxury, the width of the market, and time - and analyse how each works on the responsiveness of buyers.

blocks.heading: Five determinants, one channel
blocks.text: The main determinants of PED are the availability and closeness of substitute goods, the proportion of income the purchase takes, whether the good is a necessity or a luxury, the width of the market defined, and the length of time since the price changed. Each works through the same channel: it decides how easily a buyer can leave the good behind.

blocks.heading: How each determinant works
blocks.text: Substitutes: where close alternatives are easy to switch to, a price rise tends to push buyers towards them, so demand is price-elastic - one brand of cooking oil in a Windhoek supermarket competes with others on the same shelf. Share of income: a good taking a small slice of a budget, like salt or matches, tends to carry inelastic demand, because even a large percentage rise changes the weekly bill little; an Etosha Gate lodge stay takes a large slice, so demand there tends to respond sharply to its price. Necessity against luxury: a necessity, like the medicine a clinic in Gobabis dispenses, is bought even at a higher price - inelastic; a luxury can be postponed - elastic. Width of market: demand for "fruit juice in Oshakati" is more elastic than demand for "fruit", because narrowing the market stacks substitutes beside it. Time: after a price change, habits and contracts hold buyers where they are, so demand looks inelastic at first and grows more responsive as people adjust.

blocks.heading: The number is not the explanation
blocks.text: The confusion learners make: what PED was and what determined it are treated as the same question. The boundary: the calculation of PED is arithmetic on two percentage changes; the determinants are the features of the product and its market that explain why the arithmetic came out at that size. The test: ask whether the sentence names a number or a market feature. "PED is 1.25" answers what it was; "demand is elastic because three substitute brands sit on the same shelf" answers what made it so.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The substitute goods named here are the same substitutes that shift demand curves in topic 2.3, and the time dimension returns with supply in topic 2.8.
